blocks.text: 1. Sequence-to-Sequence Learning

blocks.alt: An input sequence goes through an encoder and decoder to produce an output sequence

blocks.text: Time Steps, the previous topic, established the basic unit sequences get processed in. Sequence-to-Sequence Learning covers how to map one entire sequence to another, a genuinely important, richer task explored throughout this topic.
Input and output sequences that can genuinely differ in length, unlike simpler, fixed-output tasks, define the genuinely core challenge covered throughout the rest of this topic.
2. Recapping The Length Mismatch Challenge

blocks.alt: A short input sequence can map to a long output sequence

blocks.text: This connects back to variable-length sequences, already covered in Sequence Data. A genuinely input sequence and a genuinely output sequence do not need to share the same length at all.

This is a genuinely real, practical challenge that Sequence-to-Sequence Learning directly addresses, extending the variable-length idea already covered there to genuinely two separate sequences at once.
3. A Preview Of Example Tasks

blocks.alt: Translation, summarization, and captioning are example sequence-to-sequence tasks

blocks.text: Genuinely common, real examples include translating a sentence from one language to another, where genuinely different word counts are likely between the two languages.

Summarizing a long document into a genuinely much shorter summary is another genuine example, sharing the exact same core structure: a genuinely long input sequence, a genuinely different-length output sequence.

blocks.text: 4. A Preview Of The Encoder-Decoder Architecture

This connects back to the encoder-decoder structure, already covered in Semantic Segmentation. The genuinely standard approach uses an encoder to read the input sequence, then a decoder to generate the output sequence.
This is covered in complete depth in the very next topic of this module, extending the encoder-decoder pattern already covered there from images to genuinely sequence data instead.
5. The Context Vector Concept

blocks.alt: An encoder compresses the input sequence into a context vector

blocks.text: A genuinely important intermediate representation connects back to the hidden state preview, already covered in Time Steps. The encoder genuinely compresses the entire input sequence into one summary, often called a context vector.
This directly builds on the hidden state idea already previewed there, extending it into a genuinely complete, final summary representing the entire input sequence at once.
6. The Decoder Starts From The Context

blocks.alt: A decoder starts from the context vector to produce the first output token

blocks.text: This connects back to sequential word generation, already covered in Image Captioning. The decoder genuinely starts from that context vector, then generates the output sequence one time step at a time.
This is exactly the sequential generation process already covered there, now applied to genuinely full sequence output, rather than just a single caption already covered in that earlier topic.

blocks.text: 7. The Information Bottleneck Issue

blocks.alt: A long input sequence gets squeezed into one vector

blocks.text: A genuinely real, honest limitation connects back to the context vector, already covered in this topic. Compressing a genuinely long input sequence into one single, fixed-size vector can genuinely lose important information.

This genuinely real bottleneck, already covered in this section, becomes especially severe for genuinely long input sequences, where a single fixed-size summary struggles to retain every genuinely important detail.
8. A Preview Of The Attention Solution

This connects back to a preview of Attention, already covered in Image Captioning and DETR. Attention Mechanism, covered later in this course, genuinely addresses this exact bottleneck already covered in the previous section.

It lets the decoder genuinely look back at different parts of the input directly, rather than relying on one single compressed vector, a genuinely direct, elegant fix explored in complete depth in that later module.

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing When Sequence-to-Sequence Learning Is Genuinely Necessary

blocks.alt: Needing to map one sequence to another points toward sequence-to-sequence learning

blocks.text: This connects back to Machine Translation, already previewed in this topic. Input and output genuinely differ in language and often in length, exactly what this topic addresses.

Text summarization, or genuinely any task mapping one sequence to a genuinely different sequence, is another genuine case where Sequence-to-Sequence Learning, already covered, is genuinely the right framework.
10. Worked Example

The example below directly demonstrates a genuinely simplified Sequence-to-Sequence pipeline, compressing an input sequence into a context vector and generating a genuinely different-length output, illustrating the concepts already covered throughout this topic.

code.content:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.RandomState(42)

input_sequence = ["the", "cat", "sat", "on", "the", "mat"]  # already covered as a variable-length input
context_vector = rng.normal(size=8)  # already covered as the context vector concept in this topic

def generate_output_word(context, previous_words, rng):
    # a genuinely simplified stand-in for a real decoder, already covered in this topic
    vocabulary = ["le", "chat", "etait", "assis", "sur", "le", "tapis", "END"]
    if len(previous_words) >= len(vocabulary) - 1:
        return "END"
    return vocabulary[len(previous_words)]

output_sequence = []
while True:
    next_word = generate_output_word(context_vector, output_sequence, rng)
    if next_word == "END":
        break
    output_sequence.append(next_word)

print(f"Input sequence ({len(input_sequence)} time steps): {' '.join(input_sequence)}")
print(f"Output sequence ({len(output_sequence)} time steps): {' '.join(output_sequence)}")
print("\nNotice the input and output genuinely differ in length, already covered as this topic's own core challenge")

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: Sequence-to-Sequence Learning maps one entire input sequence to a different output sequence.
Input and output sequences do not need to share the same length.
Machine translation and text summarization are common example tasks.
The standard approach uses an encoder to read the input, then a decoder to generate the output.
The encoder compresses the entire input into a fixed-size context vector.
The decoder starts from that context vector and generates output one time step at a time.
Compressing a long input into one fixed-size vector can lose important information.
Attention Mechanism, covered later in this course, directly addresses this information bottleneck.
Next up: Teacher Forcing, a training technique used when generating sequential output.
